intro:
This last track puts the whole course together. It starts from the café of the first lesson, where one log of payments was the record and every other number was a copy worked out from it. Then it asks how to keep a whole company's copies right: the search box, the shop owners' takings, the fraud check, the screen on a phone, the nightly payouts and the backups. And at the end it asks what the people in those records are owed.

By the end, you can:

- trace every copy of a fact back to one system of record, and change a table worked out from a log by replaying the log into a second version while the first keeps serving;
- find the same machinery inside a database, take it out, and make a read wait for its own write;
- carry one ID from a tap on a phone to the place where the money moves, so a retry can never pay twice;
- keep a rule like "one owner per handle" with one decider in a log, move money between two parts of a system with no coordinator, and tell a late answer from a wrong one;
- catch silent bugs by rebuilding a view and comparing it, find the drifted part of a huge view with a tree of hashes, and show that a log wasn't rewritten;
- spot unfairness that comes in through proxies, treat personal data as a risk to keep small, name the main laws as of November 2026, and erase a person from logs that never change.

The six lessons:

1. Data integration: systems of record, lambda and kappa
2. Unbundling the database: dataflow apps and streaming databases
3. The end-to-end argument: idempotence from client to storage
4. Constraints without coordination: timeliness and integrity
5. Trust, but verify: audits, checksums and silent corruption
6. Doing the right thing: bias, privacy, consent and the law

The track leans on the whole course: the logs, partitions and keys of Messaging and logs, the change capture and event logs of Stream processing, the races and two-phase commit of Transactions, and the single order of Consistency and consensus. You don't need to remember them in detail. Each lesson names the one it builds on, and every term is explained again the first time it appears.

The labs are plain Kotlin in the `sim` module, one package per lesson (`sfz.derive.l01` to `sfz.derive.l06`), and need no Docker. They model logs, processors, crashes and retries in memory, on a scheduler that takes its order from a fixed seed, or on a pretend clock. So a month of payments, a thousand crashes or a race between 64 clients runs in about a second and gives the same counts on every laptop. Lesson 6's lab encrypts with the JDK's own `javax.crypto`. From the `labs` folder, run `./gradlew :sim:test --tests 'sfz.derive.lNN.*'` until it passes. `./gradlew :sim:solutionTest --tests 'sfz.derive.lNN.*'` runs the same tests against the finished answers, and the Try its run demos with `./gradlew :sim:demo -Pmain=<class> --console=plain -q`.
cheatsheet:
## Words this track defines

| Term | Meaning | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| System of record | where a fact is written first; it wins every disagreement | 1 |
| Derived data | written only from the system of record's log, so it can be dropped and rebuilt | 1 |
| Total order | one sequence for all events; one log partition gives one, and one machine's speed caps it | 1 |
| Lambda, kappa | every answer worked out twice (a batch layer and a speed layer) and added when asked; one stream job replayed from a log that is kept | 1 |
| Reprocessing | new code over old input into a second version, with readers moved over a few at a time | 1 |
| Unbundling, federation | one log of writes feeding separate stores; one query that reads many stores as they are | 2 |
| Write path, read path | work done when data arrives; work done when someone asks | 2 |
| End-to-end argument | spotting repeats, checking for damage and encrypting are complete only at the two ends | 3 |
| Request ID | one ID per user intent, made on the phone, carried to a unique constraint at the final write | 3 |
| Dedupe window | how long IDs are remembered; a retry after that counts as new | 3 |
| Partition key | decides which partition, and so which single decider, sees a record | 4 |
| Timeliness, integrity | up-to-date reads (problems heal if you wait); nothing lost, made up or contradictory (problems stay) | 4 |
| Invariant confluence | a rule that copies can each keep alone and still keep after their changes merge | 4 |
| Compensating action | the apology that repairs a rule checked late: a refund, a voucher, a rebooking | 4 |
| Audit, reconciliation | rebuild a view and compare it key by key; compare totals (an alarm, not an audit) | 5 |
| Merkle tree, hash chain | hashes over key ranges, for cheap comparison; each entry holding the hash of the one before | 5 |
| Transparency log, data contract | a Merkle log anyone can check; a machine-checked promise about a dataset | 5 |
| Proxy, feedback loop | an input that stands in for a protected group; decisions changing tomorrow's training data | 6 |
| Crypto-shredding, erasure ledger | erase by destroying a per-person key; a record of erasures applied again on every restore | 6 |

## Patterns

| Problem | Pattern | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| Keep a search index, a cache and a warehouse in step with the database | change data capture into one log; every store reads it | 1, 2 |
| Change a derived table's shape | a second job from offset 0 into version 2, readers moved by a hash of their ID, version 1 kept until everyone has moved | 1 |
| A replay puts a month into today | group by event time, never by processing time | 1 |
| A user can't see their own write in the view | the write returns its offset; the read waits until the view has applied it | 2 |
| A retried request moves money twice | an ID made on the phone, and `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` in the same transaction as the money movement | 3 |
| Keep a value unique at scale | key the log by that value; one processor per partition decides in order | 4 |
| Move money between partitions without two-phase commit | append one request; the sending side's processor takes the money and writes a credit with the same ID; the receiving side drops repeats | 4 |
| A rule that may be broken for a while | check late and repair with a compensating action; check first before anything you can't undo | 4 |
| Find drift in a view | replay the log into a fresh view and compare key by key; a Merkle tree when the views live apart | 5 |
| Show that history wasn't rewritten | a hash chain, with its head published where the owner can't change it | 5 |
| Bad data from another team | data quality checks and a data contract, run by both sides; stop the line when one fails | 5 |
| Erase a person from logs you can't edit | a key per person (crypto-shredding), personal data kept out of events, compaction forced in time, old table versions expired, an erasure ledger | 6 |

## Dates as of November 2026 (not legal advice)

| Rule | From |
|---|---|
| GDPR: erasure without undue delay (Art. 17), automated decisions (Art. 22) | 25 May 2018 |
| EDPB report on the right to erasure: backups and anonymization named as problems | published 18 February 2026 |
| California CCPA rules: risk assessments, security audits, automated decision-making (ADMT) | 1 January 2026; ADMT duties for significant decisions 1 January 2027 |
| California Delete Act: data brokers process DROP deletion requests at least every 45 days | 1 August 2026 |
| EU AI Act Article 50: tell people they are dealing with AI | 2 August 2026 |
| EU AI Act high-risk: Annex III (hiring, credit scoring); Annex I (regulated products) | 2 December 2027; 2 August 2028 |
| EU Data Act | 12 September 2025; access by design 12 September 2026; no cloud switching charges from 12 January 2027 |

## Questions to ask of any flow of data

1. Which store is the system of record for each fact, and what feeds every other copy? Could you drop each copy and rebuild it?
2. Where does the single order of events stop, and which rules relate records that no one partition sees?
3. Which ID makes a retry harmless, who makes it, and where is it checked? How long is it remembered?
4. For each rule: does it need one decider (a unique index, one partition), or can it be checked late and put right?
5. Which reads need to see their own write, and how do they wait for it?
6. What rebuilds each view and compares it, and who holds the head of the audit log?
7. For each automated decision: what is recorded, who can overturn it, and are error rates measured for each group?
8. For each copy of a person's data: how does a deletion reach it, how long does that take, and what happens on a restore?

## How the whole course fits together

The course started in a café, with one picture: a log of payments as the system of record, and every other number a copy worked out from it, judged by how fast it answers, how it fails and how much load it carries. The networking and operating-systems tracks showed the machinery under every one of those numbers. On one machine, data models, storage engines, caches and encodings turned records into bytes, indexes and views that a single computer can find fast and keep through a crash. Across machines, replication made copies, partitioning split the data, and transactions kept writers from breaking rules. Faults, time and truth showed what goes wrong when networks, clocks and programs misbehave, and consensus let machines agree on one order anyway. The last part moved data between systems: logs gave every reader the same order, and stream and batch processing worked out new data from it. This track joined it all into one design. A log is the system of record and everything else is derived, kept right end to end by request IDs, single deciders and audits, and by the care owed to the people the records describe. The café owner's 49.00 and 9.00 were the first copy and the first record; the questions above work for every system after it.
recap: Name one system of record for each fact, and feed every other store from its log with change data capture. A derived store is written only from that log, so it can be dropped and rebuilt.
One order for everything stops at one machine's speed, at regions, at separate teams' programs and at offline phones. Past that, keep order per key and write causal links into the data.
Change a derived table's shape by replaying the kept log into a second version, grouped by event time. Move readers over a few at a time, and keep the old version until the last reader leaves.

Indexes, replicas and views are all built by snapshot, catch up, keep up. Unbundling runs that machinery as readers of one log of writes. Streaming databases keep views for you and are still behind, so a read that needs its own write waits for its offset.

Each layer's guard against repeats stops at its own edge. One ID per user intent, made on the phone and checked by a unique constraint together with the money movement, is what takes duplicates to zero.

A unique value needs one decider: key the log by that value. A transfer between partitions is one appended request plus a debit and a credit worked out from it, with repeats dropped by ID and no two-phase commit.

Timeliness problems heal if you wait; integrity problems stay. Guarantee integrity everywhere, buy timeliness where someone is waiting, and check late with an apology wherever a rule is invariant confluent or the apology is cheap.

Hardware, databases and your own code corrupt data silently. Rebuild views and compare them, compare far-apart views with Merkle trees, chain the log's hashes and publish its head, and check data where it crosses from one team to another.

Automated decisions repeat the unfairness in their data through proxies and feedback loops. Record each decision's inputs and reasons, measure errors for each group, and keep a person who can overturn it. Personal data is a risk: collect less, and give it an end date.

Erasure must reach every copy: topics, compaction, old table versions, views and backups. Crypto-shredding makes copies you can't edit unreadable, every restore must apply the erasure record again, and whether a deleted key counts as erasure in law is still open. None of this is legal advice.

quiz.q: The team wants a derived table of daily takings to show each shop's takings per hour instead, with no downtime and a way back. What do you do?
options: Change the table in place over a weekend, with commands that alter and update every row
Run a second copy of the job from offset 0 into a new table, move readers over a few at a time, and retire the old table only when everyone has moved
Add the new columns to the speed layer, and add them to the batch layer's answer when someone asks
Have the app write the new shape alongside the old one
quiz.why: That's the reprocessing recipe from Data integration. The log is kept, so a second job can build version 2 next to version 1, readers move over a share at a time, and version 1 stays as the way back until it's retired. Having the app write both shapes is a dual write, two writes that can fail apart, and changing the table in place leaves no way back.

quiz.q: A stream job replayed from the log puts a whole month of payments into today's takings. What went wrong?
options: The log wasn't kept long enough
The job ran with exactly-once processing switched off
The job groups payments by processing time, which during a replay is "now" for every record
The partitions were read out of order
quiz.why: During a replay every record is processed now, so grouping by processing time puts everything into the window that holds the replay's own time. Grouping by the event time stored in each record puts each payment on the day it happened.

quiz.q: A user changes their payout account, and the settings page, which reads a view kept by a streaming database, still shows the old one. Which fix keeps the view as the place reads come from?
options: Ask the view for updates more often
Write to the view directly from the app
Return the write's position in the log (its offset), and make the read wait until the view has applied it
Keep the old value in a cache for a shorter time
quiz.why: The view is derived and always a little behind. Waiting for the write's own offset gives read-your-writes to the reads that need it, and costs the others nothing. Asking more often shrinks the gap without closing it, and writing to the view directly turns it into a second system of record.

quiz.q: A pipeline has TCP, Kafka's idempotent producer and Kafka's exactly-once processing, and it still writes duplicate ledger rows when a phone retries a transfer. What fixes it?
options: An ID made on the phone, carried through every hop, and checked by a unique constraint in the same transaction as the ledger write
Turning on exactly-once in the consumer as well
Longer timeouts on the phone, so that it retries less
A `SELECT` for an existing row before the `INSERT`
quiz.why: Each layer drops repeats only of its own resends, and the phone's retry is a new request to all of them. Only an ID for the user's intent, checked where the money finally moves, recognises it. A `SELECT` before the `INSERT` is check-then-insert and fails at read committed, and longer timeouts make duplicates rarer, not impossible.

quiz.q: A program reading a log keeps request IDs, chosen by the customer's app, unique per shop. Which partition key makes that correct?
options: Payment number
Customer ID
Shop ID and request ID together
A random key, to spread the load evenly
quiz.why: Every request that could clash must reach the same single decider, so the key must be exactly the value the rule is about. Keyed by payment number or customer ID, two requests with the same request ID can land in two partitions, and both are accepted.

quiz.q: Which of these needs one decider, rather than a check after the fact?
options: Every payment amount is above zero
Every new refund points to a payment that exists
A wallet's balance never goes below zero
Payout IDs are unique, made by each region from its own range
quiz.why: A balance with a floor, pushed down by withdrawals, is not invariant confluent: two regions can each spend the last 50.00. Value checks, new rows that point to existing ones, and IDs from separate ranges all merge safely. A business may still choose to check the balance late and repair it with an overdraft fee, which is an apology by design.

quiz.q: An hourly check shows that the sum of balances equals the sum of postings, yet the hourly audit that rebuilds every account finds two accounts wrong. How can both be true?
options: The audit has a bug: if the totals match, every account matches
Two errors of opposite sign cancel in the total, but not account by account
The total check ran before the audit
The Merkle tree hashed the wrong ranges
quiz.why: A total is one number, so +16 in one account and -16 in another leave it unchanged. That's why sums and counts are alarms, and only the key-by-key rebuild is an audit.

quiz.q: An insider rewrites one old ledger entry and works out every later hash in the chain again. What still catches it?
options: Working out the chain again from the first entry
The check number (CRC) stored with the rewritten record
The head hash the auditors received before the rewrite
Nothing
quiz.why: A chain that was fully worked out again agrees with itself, and a CRC is as easy to work out again as a hash. A head held by someone the insider can't reach no longer matches. Transparency logs such as Certificate Transparency rely on the same idea, with monitors keeping the tree heads they have seen.

quiz.q: A fraud model never reads the customer's group, yet blocks honest customers in one neighbourhood three times as often as elsewhere. What is the most likely mechanism, and the first thing to do?
options: Chance; train it again with a new random seed
A proxy, such as a postcode score learned from unfair past investigations; measure error rates for each group, and test the model without the proxy
Too little training data; collect more of the same labels
The cut-off is too strict; loosen it for everyone
quiz.why: Inputs that go along with the group carry the unfairness of the records they were learned from, and more of the same labels repeats it. Measuring false-positive rates for each group finds it. A model without the proxy can often catch about as much fraud with even error rates, as the demo in Doing the right thing showed.

quiz.q: Personal fields in an event log are encrypted with a key per customer, and a customer has been erased by deleting their key. Which event brings their data back?
options: Replaying the event log from offset 0
Compacting the topic
Expiring old versions of the Iceberg table
Restoring the key store from a backup taken before the erasure, without applying the erasure record again
quiz.why: A replay with the key gone shows the customer as erased, and compaction or expiring old versions only remove more. An old key backup still holds the deleted key, so a restore makes every event readable again, unless it forgets everyone in the erasure ledger afterwards. That's what the EDPB asks for with backups that can't be edited.
